title: Total dots on screen is the wall, not draw calls: merging bought nothing, thinning the authored three took 1,200 bodies from 22.5% late frames to 0.1%
context: The owner compared four runs by screenshot because there was no way to control across runs, and every card showed PEAK CALLS 0 with GPU timing unavailable. They asked which optimisations to implement — merged dot clouds, temporal spreading, shader pre-compile, all of them — and floated dropping to a cheaper gunship orbital view when frame cost rises.
outcome: The cards were from a stale service-worker cache: the current build records calls and falls back to a stalling probe when EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 is absent, verified by blocking the extension through Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument (49 samples, 306 calls, no timer). Every run record now carries the build tag and whether the timer was present, and a card whose run recorded no draw calls says 'stale build — reload with ?sw=0' rather than showing zeros. A sweep button runs 250/500/1000/1200 back to back keeping every leg, so a comparison is a series under one build in one sitting. Measured with that: 250 bodies 306 calls 123,500 points 0.1% late; 500 556/247,000 2.2%; 1000 1,056/494,000 19.6%; 1200 1,256/592,800 23.7%. Merging was then implemented as src/fx/dot-swarm.js, an InstancedBufferGeometry crowd in ONE draw call, and it REFUTED the hypothesis: 1,256 calls to 146 at 1200 bodies changed nothing and was worse at the top (late 23.7% to 47.7%), because dead instances still run the vertex shader while hidden objects are culled outright. Draw calls are not the constraint at this scale. Point count is: 1,200 ghosts at 180,000 points drop 0.1% of frames while 1,200 phages at 592,800 drop 22.5%, at identical draw calls. The lever is therefore the density factor, which the three authored creatures ignored — the densest bodies on the roster (692, 494, 578 against 150) were the only ones a crowd could not turn down. creatures.thinCloud resamples them uniformly (keeping index i only when it opens a new bucket, so each section keeps its share rather than a slice taking the phage's head and dropping its legs) and DOT_SHAPES routes the three through it; the authored count stays the ceiling because interpolating new dots would be invention. Result at 1,200 phages: density 1.0 is 592,800 points and 22.5% late, 0.5 is 296,400 and 9.6%, 0.3 is 177,600 and 0.1% — a locked 60fps at the same population that was failing.
alternatives: Adopt merged instancing: rejected on its own measurement. src/fx/dot-swarm.js is kept because it is correct and the technique becomes right if draw calls ever do bind, but it buys nothing today and costs the per-body material the game writes to every frame for the slow field and the death fade.
Temporal spreading of enemy updates: not implemented, simulation is not the bottleneck — 505 concurrent held 60fps in the real game and the cost here tracks points, not logic.
Resolution LOD by crowd size: superseded by density. Thinning the bodies attacks the same vertex work without touching the framebuffer everything else is drawn into.

Switching to a cheaper gunship view when cost rises: not implemented; the trigger would fire hardest at the climax and teach the player to read the frame budget. The inversion — raise density because the cheap scheduled view is arriving — keeps the causality the fiction already has.
evidence: Sweep under one build: 250/500/1000/1200 at 0.1/2.2/19.6/23.7% late frames, medians 16.7 to 16.9 ms throughout.
Merged vs per-object at 1200 bodies: 146 vs 1,256 draw calls, late frames 47.7% vs 23.7%.

test/thin-cloud.mjs: the three honour the factor, the authored count is a ceiling, each section keeps its share, a thinned cloud is never empty and never grows, thinning is deterministic, and highlight dots survive.
npm test, npm run check, npm run build, npm run test:browser and node scripts/browser-test.mjs --dist all pass.
